title: How I Teach: Cells at KS4
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino explains how she rebuilt her teaching of cells after noticing students kept forgetting organelle functions despite a textbook-style sequence. She starts from the questions students must answer and from what organisms need to survive, so that cells have a purpose. She then introduces organelles gradually, drawing them one at a time, with cold calling and mini-whiteboard quizzes between steps. She delays the nucleus, avoids the misleading brain of the cell analogy, and moves from simple cells to eukaryotes and then prokaryotes. The sequence ends with recall and application questions in lessons and homework. It is a concrete, reasoned walk-through of explicit-instruction sequencing for a science topic.
points: Opening with what organisms need to survive gives students a purpose that organelles can then be hung on.
Introducing structures one at a time and quizzing recall with mini-whiteboards before adding more controls the load.
She avoids the brain of the cell analogy because she found she was the one introducing the misconception.
Application questions, such as inferring cell type from organelles, test understanding beyond recall.
quotes: I now teach cells in a different way. I am sure I will tweak this method further as time goes on.
By doing this, I try to get the point of cells across. Cells are not random units of life. They have a purpose and everything we will learn about them helps the cell achieve that purpose.

Before I check that students can recall these structures, I say that we use the word organelles to describe them. Next, I conduct a mini-whiteboard quiz and ask students various questions to see if they can recall the names and functions of these 4 organelles.

This is when I describe the function of the nucleus itself: it controls the cell’s activities and it contains the genetic material. In the past, I would also say that it is not the brain of the cell. But by doing this, I have found that I was the one introducing this idea and so I refrain from mentioning it.
At this point, I quiz students again. This tends to be a quick mini-whiteboard quiz, with questions from earlier in the sequence mixed with questions about the new information.

This sequence so far can take more than a lesson. To check understanding, I provide lots of questions, where students can practice recall but also apply their knowledge. These are given both in lesson and as homework.
